transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. I appreciate you taking the time. You know, I wasn't even sure I should come in, but... well, honestly, I'm starting to drive myself a little crazy. What brings me in is I just keep forgetting things. And I mean things I really, really shouldn’t be forgetting. 

Like my heart follow-up appointments. That's important stuff, right? You don't mess around with the ticker, but the day just comes and goes and it completely vanishes from my mind. And then the clinic leaves a voicemail, and I listen to it, and I tell myself, 'Okay, I'll call them right back just as soon as I finish fixing this hinge on the back door.' But then I get sidetracked doing something else, and three days go by, and I still haven't called the clinic back! It’s embarrassing, it really is. 

And it happens with my little projects, too. I try to keep busy these days since I'm not working anymore, do a little repair work around the house or for the neighbors, just to keep my hands moving. But I’ll get all geared up, walk over to a buddy's house to help him out, and realize I showed up without the right tools for the repair job. I'll have left the exact socket wrench I needed sitting right on my kitchen counter because I was thinking about something else on my way out the door. It's just a constant string of things like that, all day long, and it's getting so frustrating...
Have you noticed problems like this with forgetfulness and losing focus going back to when you were a child or young adult, or is this a new change for you?

Oh, it is definitely not new. Not by a long shot. If my mother were still around, God rest her soul, she would probably laugh out loud at that question. I mean, going all the way back to when I was just a little guy in grade school... I remember Mrs. Gable's class—or wait, maybe it was Mrs. Higgins? No, Higgins was fourth grade, Gable was third. Anyway, even back then, I was always the kid who just could not, for the life of me, stay in his seat. 

It was like I had a motor running inside me that just wouldn't shut off. The teacher would be up there at the chalkboard, trying to explain fractions or whatever it was, and I would just blurt out the answers before she even finished asking the question. I was never trying to be a bad kid or disrespectful, you know? It is just that the thought popped into my head and it had to come right out my mouth that exact second. 

And the talking... oh boy, the talking. I got so many notes sent home in my lunchbox for talking too much to the kids next to me. My dad used to sit me down at the kitchen table, look at one of those notes from the teacher, and tell me that my mouth was going a mile a minute while my brain was still at the starting line. So, yeah, this whole thing with my mind bouncing around and not being able to just sit still and rein it in... it has been the story of my life, really, from grade school all the way up to now. It just feels a little more embarrassing now that I'm an old man forgetting my heart appointments, you know?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong pattern (from grade school through adulthood) of significant inattentive symptoms (forgetting important appointments, losing/misplacing needed items, being easily sidetracked, difficulty completing tasks) combined with childhood-onset hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (inability to stay seated, blurting out answers, excessive talking). Symptoms began before age 12, have persisted across settings and developmental stages, and currently cause functional impairment (missed medical follow-ups, incomplete home repair tasks). This presentation is consistent with combined-type ADHD (ICD-10 F90.0, Disturbance of activity and attention), rather than a primarily inattentive-only pattern or an acquired cognitive disorder such as dementia, which is less likely given the lifelong trajectory and absence of progressive cognitive decline.
